In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

dirithromycin does not form a type I binding or a metabolic intermediate spectrum with human cytochrome P450 enzymes, but it is possible that dirithromycylamine may be formed in vivo and may be responsible for the clinically reported interaction of dirithromycin.
troleandomycin forms a type I spectrum with all microsomal preparations tested and a metabolic intermediate spectrum with all but one human liver microsomal preparation.

dirithromycin does not appear to form a type I binding complex with cytochrome P 450 in either rat or human liver microsomes, but does form a small metabolic intermediate-type complex in dexamethasome-pretreated rat liver microsomes.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

dirithromycin does not form a type I binding or a metabolic intermediate cytochrome P450 complex in rat or human liver microsomes, suggesting that this macrolide will be less prone than other macrolide antibiotics to cause drug-drug interactions.
troleandomycin is the most potent macrolide inhibitor of cytochrome P450, followed by erythromycin and erythrymycin N-demethylase.
dirithromycin is a poor inducer of cytochrome P450 and a poor inhibitor of cytochrome 3A4.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the human liver microsomal system may not be a good model to predict the formation of a metabolic intermediate complex with macrolide antibiotics.
the human metabolic intermediate complexes for troleandomycin are larger than those for dirithromycin in microsomes obtained after barbiturate therapy.

the formation of a type I binding spectra and a metabolic intermediate complexes are useful in vitro markers of the potential for drug interactions with macrolide antibiotics, but the absence of such markers does not rule out such interactions.
